clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal dominant red-cell membrane disorder within the hereditary stomatocytosis family, characterised by a temperature-dependent cation leak that worsens on cooling.
Most classic cases are caused by variants in SLC4A1, encoding band 3 (anion exchanger 1, AE1), which convert the anion exchanger into an abnormal cation-leak pathway.
It presents with variable compensated or overt haemolytic anaemia, splenomegaly and, on the blood film, stomatocytes with occasional target cells.
A hallmark laboratory artefact is pseudohyperkalaemia, as potassium leaks from red cells into plasma when a sample is stored at room temperature or cooled before separation.
Red-cell indices often show a raised mean cell volume, and cation-flux studies demonstrate the characteristic temperature-dependent leak.
Splenectomy is generally contraindicated in the stomatocytoses because of a markedly increased risk of thromboembolic complications.

A distinct variant, stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis, is caused by SLC2A1 (GLUT1) variants and combines haemolysis with neurological features such as seizures, cognitive impairment and movement disorder, together with cataracts.
Iron overload can develop even without heavy transfusion and should be monitored.
reference.pathophysiology: Cryohydrocytosis is a hereditary stomatocytosis caused by an abnormal monovalent cation (sodium and potassium) leak across the red-cell membrane that is markedly temperature-dependent, increasing as the cell is cooled. In the classic form, dominant missense variants in SLC4A1 (band 3 / anion exchanger 1) convert the normally tightly gated anion transporter into a poorly regulated cation-conductance pathway, so that sodium enters and potassium leaves the cell; the resulting cation and water fluxes alter cell hydration and shorten red-cell survival, producing haemolysis. The same in-vitro leak underlies pseudohyperkalaemia when blood is not promptly processed at body temperature. A separate but clinically overlapping entity, stomatin-deficient cryohydrocytosis, arises from variants in SLC2A1 (GLUT1); because GLUT1 is also essential for glucose transport across the blood-brain barrier, these patients additionally show a Glut1-deficiency neurological phenotype with epilepsy, developmental problems and cataracts, alongside secondary loss of the membrane protein stomatin.
additionalDifferentials: Dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis / hereditary xerocytosis (PIEZO1, KCNN4)
Hereditary spherocytosis, including other band 3 (SLC4A1) phenotypes
Autoimmune and other acquired haemolytic anaemias
Sitosterolaemia and other rare membrane or stomatocytic disorders
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film for stomatocytes, target cells and a raised mean cell volume
Reticulocyte count and haemolysis markers, including bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and haptoglobin
Paired plasma potassium measured promptly and after delayed or cool storage to demonstrate pseudohyperkalaemia
Red-cell cation flux studies and osmotic gradient ektacytometry across a range of temperatures
Molecular testing of SLC4A1 and, when neurological features are present, SLC2A1, with PIEZO1, KCNN4 and RHAG for the differential
Iron studies and ferritin to detect iron overload
Direct antiglobulin test to exclude immune haemolysis
redFlags: Progressive iron overload with organ dysfunction
Neurological features such as seizures or movement disorder, suggesting the SLC2A1/GLUT1 variant
Spurious hyperkalaemia prompting inappropriate emergency treatment
reference.prognosis: Anaemia is often mild and compensated with a generally good outlook; the main hazards are iatrogenic post-splenectomy thrombosis and transfusion- or absorption-related iron overload, while the GLUT1-related variant carries the added morbidity of its neurological disease.
pitfalls: Acting on pseudohyperkalaemia and giving unnecessary emergency treatment for a spurious result
Performing splenectomy, which markedly raises thrombotic risk in the stomatocytoses
Misclassifying the disorder as hereditary spherocytosis and proceeding to splenectomy
Overlooking iron overload because transfusion requirements are low
Missing the SLC2A1/GLUT1 variant when neurological features accompany the haemolysis
